extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and avoidance of common a priori fallacies and natural prejudices in philosophical and scientific reasoning; aimed at improving how laws and causes are inferred from language, intuition, or pure reason instead of experience. Covers specific errors (reification, undue reliance on language, single-cause assumptions, resemblance-based inferences) with historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of general terms / Mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that names of qualities or general terms denote distinct outward entities (e.g., 'whiteness' as an entity; 'man in general' as an abstract or universal man). Described as ascribing objective existence to subjective creations of our own faculties — 'Mysticism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating abstract/general language as evidence of distinct real entities. The text warns this elevates general substances to 'the only subjects of science' and thwarts intelligible discussion; examples include τὸ ὄν and τὸ ἔν being treated as peculiar entities. Anti-pattern: inferring ontological status from grammatical or conceptual distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Sufficient Reason (misapplied a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting that a phenomenon must follow a certain law because we see no reason why it should deviate — i.e., concluding what is natural from the absence of a reason to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer physical laws merely because alternatives seem arbitrary without empirical evidence. Examples: attempted a priori proofs of inertia and the first law of motion (arguing a body at rest must remain so because there's no reason to move in one direction rather than another). The text treats such uses as fallacious and recommends experience as the only real proof of laws of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to a priori reasoning instead of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to establish general facts of the outward world by pure reasoning (without appeal to experience), as done by some geometers and philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer empirical evidence over pure a priori demonstration when establishing physical laws. The text cites Archimedes and geometers who 'borrow no principle from experiment' and criticizes treating such premises as more scientific than familiar experience. Anti-pattern: privileging deductive elegance over experimental confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming linguistic distinctions map to natural divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudice that differences in nature must correspond to the distinctions of common language — that classes made by popular phrases are natural classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of letting ordinary language categories determine scientific classification. The text criticizes Greek philosophers for treating language-made classes as natural, and warns this leads to analyzing notions instead of facts. Example: treating meanings inferred from 'in' or other common words as evidential for physical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Contrarieties (inferring nature from linguistic oppositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that adjectives or substances opposed in common language point to a fundamental antithesis in nature (e.g., Limited/Unlimited, Odd/Even, One/Many leading to metaphysical dogmas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deriving ontological or physical principles from mere contrasts present in language or abstract conception. The text gives Aristotle and Pythagorean examples where oppositions in language produced unwarranted doctrines (four elements, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming single, invariant cause (Baconian 'forma')
rubrics_metrics.description: The tacit assumption that a phenomenon has one single cause or invariable condition present in all instances (Bacon's search for a single 'forma').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for plurality of causes; do not use methods that implicitly assume uniqueness of cause (e.g., eliminating negatives to isolate one 'forma'). The text argues this assumption is false for many sensible qualities and leads investigations astray (e.g., trying to find one cause for heat, color, taste). Anti-pattern: designing exclusionary tests that presuppose a lone universal cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing conditions/causes with the phenomenon itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking as if the conditions or causes of a phenomenon were identical to the phenomenon (e.g., treating heat as 'a kind of motion' in language that makes no distinction between heat and its conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a clear conceptual separation between an effect (phenomenon as experienced) and the physical conditions or mechanisms that produce it. Text examples: Bacon's language in 'inquisitio in formam calidi' and Darwin's Zoonomia describing ideas as 'contraction, motion, or configuration' of fibres—both blur effect and cause and are criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming causes and effects must resemble one another ('like produces like')
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy that the conditions of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon itself (e.g., Doctrine of Signatures; assuming properties of elements must resemble properties of compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not select hypotheses or remedies merely because they bear superficial resemblance to the desired effect. The text documents medical and magical examples (turmeric for jaundice, poppies for head complaints, charms) and warns that resemblance-based guesses often produce false theories (alchemy, spurious physiological mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming homogeneity between causes and effects (perfections transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding that the Efficient Cause must have all the perfections of the effect, or that an effect cannot surpass its cause (Descartes' and Cicero's versions of the idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reasoning that requires causes to contain every property of their effects. The text criticizes such principles (Descartes: 'the Efficient Cause must at least have all the perfections of the effect'; Cicero's complaint that an effect cannot be greater than its cause) as gratuitous assumptions leading to errors about causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting cross-domain causation because of dissimilarity (mind/matter interaction denial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying the possibility of causal interaction between domains (e.g., mind and matter) on the ground they share no common property — leading to doctrines like pre-established harmony or occasional causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rule out interactions between different kinds of phenomena simply because they lack obvious common properties. The text cites Coleridge, Spinoza, Leibnitz and Malebranche as examples where such a priori denial produced elaborate but speculative theories (pre-established harmony, occasional causes), which are criticized as stemming from the same a priori fallacy.
